hypothesis.cheapest_refuting_observation: If `savedregs.py game/mb/mb_tree MBNewNode` ever reports a FIRST-definition mismatch, the values are not the same four and this framing is wrong. Measured 2026-09-03: it reports ASSIGNMENT MATCHES on all four first definitions and explicitly warns that 3 later definitions per stream are outside its scope - the later definitions are where the whole 23-word residual lives, which is a good calibration case for that tool's scope line.
hypothesis.screened_against_target: yes - both orderings and the live-range spans were read from the aligned raw view against retail bytes, and cross-checked with savedregs.py.
hypothesis.statement: The two streams assign the SAME four values to the callee-saved set in a rotated order, and the rotation follows a different ranking rule, not a different declaration order. The four defining instructions, read from the aligned raw view: @0x10 target `mr. r28,r4` against ours `mr. r29,r4` (matrix); @0x14 target `addi r31,r3,0` against ours `addi r28,r3,0` (parent); @0x18 target `addi r29,r5,0` against ours `addi r30,r5,0` (type); @0x38 target `lwz r30,0(0) @lbl_80344EE0` against ours `lwz r31,0(0) @lbl_80344EE0` (node). So ours is exactly parameter/declaration order ascending - parent r28, matrix r29, type r30, node r31 - while retail is matrix r28, type r29, node r30, parent r31, i.e. parent (the LONGEST live range, @0x14 to @0xe8 `stw r31,120(r28)` in our colouring / `stw r30,120(r31)` in retail's) takes the highest register. A priority/live-range ranking is the mechanism to attack; a declaration permutation cannot express it because the parameter order is ABI-fixed and there is only one local.
